title: Alameda Co. Supervisor Gets In Faces of ICE Agents at Santa Rita Jail, Demands They Leave
summary: Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas took a physical stand against ICE agents Monday at Santa Rita Jail, where agents were apparently looking to ensnare immigrants, including visitors at the jail.
content: Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas took a physical stand against ICE agents Monday at Santa Rita Jail, where agents were apparently looking to ensnare immigrants, including visitors at the jail. As ICE continues an apparent surge operation in the East Bay this week, Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas took it upon herself to confront masked ICE agents who were hanging around outside Santa Rita Jail, showing them the cease-and-desist letter from the county that demands ICE agents stay off of county property unless they have a judicial warrant for a specific individual. "What I saw today by ICE was absolutely horrifying," Bas says on the video seen below, standing outside the jail. "They racially profiled a family who was here visiting someone. They chased them to their car. They had a child with them." For much of the video, Bas is repeating to the agents that they should leave, showing them a copy of the cease-and-desist letter. The men, all wearing khaki cargo pants and ICE vests, most of them wearing masks covering their faces, mostly brush her off, and one at one point says, "County doesn't override federal." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nikki Fortunato Bas (@supervisor.nikkifortunatobas) The agents can be seen talking to a man off to one side near the jail entrance doors. "I am here trying to uphold the constitution and that person's right to due process," Bas says to one agent in the video. "We have no idea if what you are doing is legal, because you have not shown us a judicial warrant." Image via Nikki Fortunato Bas/Instagram The agent later tells Bas that they were seeking a specific individual, and this man "matched the description," so they questioned him and got his name. The name did not match, so they let him go. Bas suggests that it was her and other activists' intervention that helped "keep this family together," though that is not clear from the video. Over the weekend, neighbors who tried to get in the way of ICE agents in East Oakland were met with pepper spray and flash-bang grenades, sending two to the hospital. Two residents were arrested , including a teenager who reportedly wrote "ICE OUT" on the windshield of an ICE officer's vehicle, and the teen was reportedly yelling that he was under 17. Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee condemned the operation, calling the aggressive enforcement tactics “disturbing and unacceptable.” On Monday, seven mayors of cities in Contra Costa County signed an open letter to the community, telling them to stay vigilant in the midst of the ICE operations. As KRON4 reports , Assemblymember Anamarie Avilas Farias held a press conference Tuesday to warn the community, and she noted that one of her constituents picked up an assault-style magazine of bullets that an agent dropped while chasing someone in Concord. "These gestapo-like tactics have no place in our democracy," she said. Related: Family, Colleagues Fight For Release of USF Professor Missing From ICE’s Detainee Database

title: SF Zoo Mourns Its Oldest Animal, a Tortoise Who Introduced Visitors to His Species
summary: Thousands of SF Zoo visitors got to know desert tortoises through Mojave, the Zoo's 79-year-old resident who spent nearly three decades serving as an ambassador for his increasingly threatened species.
content: Thousands of SF Zoo visitors got to know desert tortoises through Mojave, the Zoo's 79-year-old resident who spent nearly three decades serving as an ambassador for his increasingly threatened species. Mojave had been living at the Zoo's Koret Animal Rescue and Conservation Center since 1997, where he became one of its longtime animal ambassadors. Through the Zoo's Wildlife Theater and Nature Trail programs, the tortoise introduced thousands of visitors, staff members, and volunteers to desert tortoises and their place in the ecosystem. The zoo shared on social media that earlier this year, a CT scan revealed that Mojave had developed a spinal condition. Keepers and veterinary hospital staff monitored him over the following months, but when the condition began affecting his quality of life, they decided to humanely euthanize him. Zoo staff were able to spend time with him and say goodbye. View this post on Instagram A post shared by San Francisco Zoo (@sanfranciscozoo) Mojave desert tortoises are a threatened keystone species that play an important role in California's desert ecosystems. They are also the official state reptile. According to the Los Angeles Times , the Mojave Desert supported hundreds of tortoises per square mile 80 years ago, with the animals found throughout nearly every part of the desert below 3,000 feet in elevation. Today, most populations in California outside designated recovery areas have reportedly dwindled to just two or three adults per square mile, making it increasingly difficult for males and females to find one another to reproduce. Despite receiving state and federal threatened-species protections in 1989 and 1990, respectively, the tortoise's numbers have continued to fall. In 2022, Defenders of Wildlife, the Desert Tortoise Council, and the Desert Tortoise Preserve Committee petitioned the California Fish and Game Commission to upgrade its status to endangered. The commission approved the change last year, as NPR reported . The designation could help direct additional resources toward conservation efforts, according to state agency spokesperson Krysten Kellum, who told NPR the change "highlights the urgency of tortoise conservation needs." But federal staffing cuts and funding freezes under the Trump administration have reportedly raised concerns about the future of those efforts. Kristina Drake, former head of the US Fish and Wildlife Service's Desert Tortoise Recovery Office, left the agency through its deferred resignation program and said she doesn't anticipate additional federal funding for the species. There have been some encouraging developments. In 2024, 70 Mojave desert tortoises were released into their native habitat at Edwards Air Force Base in Southern California through a collaborative program involving San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens, the USFWS, and the US Geological Survey. The young tortoises were raised using a combination of indoor and outdoor techniques intended to improve their survival rates. Researchers have continued monitoring the group, tracking their health and behavior, including their ability to establish and modify burrows for shelter.
